> 知不知，尚矣；不知知，病也.

Fourteen characters, and the subject is extremely concrete: calling your own score.

## 知 is an arrow that hit, and a mouth that said so

知 is built from 矢 (the arrow) and 口 (the mouth).

The arrow goes out; if it hits, a voice calls it. That is 知.

So 知's original sense is a hit — an event, not a possession. If it did not hit, it is not 知.

## Once that is right, the two clauses come alive

知不知 — he knows that this arrow did not hit.

不知知 — it did not hit, and he called it a hit.

## 病 is the illness that has worsened

病: 疾加也. 疾 is the small ailment; 病 is the one that has progressed.

So 不知知，病也 is not the mild reproach "don't pretend you know." It is a diagnosis: this is not a minor fault, it is already the advanced stage.

## Why advanced

Because a wrong score propagates. The next step is adjusting your aim against the wrong mark, and after that the whole practice is calibrated to a target that was never hit.

One false call does not stay one false call.

## 聖人不病，以其病病

The sage is not ill because he treats the illness as an illness.

病病 — the first 病 is a verb: to treat as a disease. He keeps it in the category of things that must be watched, which is why it never becomes the thing that runs him.

That is the whole method, and it is not modesty. Modesty is a manner; 病病 is a maintenance routine.

## The chapter's place

70: nobody takes it up, because it is too plain.
71: and here is the specific mechanism inside a person that keeps it that way — the mouth calling hits that did not happen.

Fourteen characters, and it is the only chapter in the book that is purely about the reliability of one's own report.

## A test

Take one thing you said you understood this week. Ask whether you could have called the hit before you made the claim, or whether the call came first and the arrow came after.
